doc.title: Artie Shaw — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Jazz, its audience and the 1953 records
title: Sidemen Rudy Tanza, Ralph Roselund and Herbie Steward; Vache and Woody Shaw
summary: Talbot and Shaw discuss his wartime saxophonists, especially Herbie Steward's musicality, and musical modern players today.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: Yeah. Beautiful. What became of him, I wonder?

I have no idea. Once the musicians came back out of this, they probably couldn’t get work. Went into something else. But [tenor saxophonist Ralph] Roselund I remember he had very good control of his horn. He could do things . . . Herbie did most of the solos. But a couple of the things I let Roselund . . . Roselund made a couple of records where he played something quite interesting.
That’s Herbie Steward, who later was with Woody Herman, yeah?

Herbie Steward. Herbie was a good player. Nice guy and really good musicality. He’s another one who had great musicality. Somebody sent me some tape of him playing clarinet. Sounds marvelous. He has a very good sound. It’s like Lester’s sound was good on the clarinet. Couldn’t do much with it, but what he did was good. Some people have that immediately. I mentioned Warren Vaché. Of the modern players today, he’s for me one of the most musical. But we talked about Woody Shaw, who’s also musical. There are a lot of very good ones around. But they don’t get the credit they deserve, because today there’s a kind of angriness going around, and they don’t meet those standards.
